ts-node type-checks by default using the TypeScript compiler, which makes it slow, and ESM support needs extra loader setup. tsx uses esbuild to strip types, so it's much faster and handles ESM/CJS interop out of the box, but it does no type checking, so keep `tsc --noEmit` for that. It also doesn't support things like decorator metadata. Action: nothing to change; I can add a typecheck script if you want type errors surfaced separately.

In Next.js, the error passed to global-error.tsx can carry a `digest`, which is the id that matches the server log entry (it's only set for errors that originated on the server). The Sentry capture there probably only sends the error, so I'll attach the digest as a tag or extra on the event. Action: read app/global-error.tsx and the Sentry setup, add `error.digest` to the captured event, and add a test that asserts it's included.

`docker compose up -d` creates the containers, networks and volumes if they don't exist (and recreates containers whose config or image changed), then starts them in the background. `docker compose start` only starts containers that already exist and are stopped, creates nothing, and won't pick up compose file changes. Action: none needed; use `up -d` after changing config and `start` to resume stopped ones.

There's a real difference. structuredClone keeps Date, Map, Set, typed arrays, undefined values, BigInt and circular references, while the JSON trick turns Dates into strings, drops undefined, turns Map/Set into empty objects, and throws on cycles and BigInt. structuredClone throws on functions and DOM nodes and drops class prototypes. Action: none; default to structuredClone (Node 17+) unless you specifically want a JSON-safe copy.
